subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Sludge: Friction That Hinders
description: A quick, practical guide to Sludge: Friction That Hinders.

hook.text: A veteran applies for benefits. The form is 20 pages, requires three IDs, and has a 45-day wait. Many give up.

buildup.text: Sludge is excessive friction that prevents people from accessing benefits or exercising rights.

discovery.text: Sunstein coined sludge to describe deliberate or negligent obstacles in bureaucratic processes that discourage.

twist.text: Some sludge is intentional. Making it hard to claim rebates or cancel subscriptions saves organizations money.

climax.text: Sludge audits identify and remove unnecessary friction. Governments should make accessing rights as easy as paying.

punchline.text: If the process is hard, ask who benefits from the friction.

quiz.question: What is sludge in behavioral policy?
options: Excessive friction that prevents people from accessing benefits or rights
A nudge that encourages healthy behavior

details.summary: Sludge is the opposite of a nudge: unnecessary friction that discourages people from accessing benefits, exercising rights, or completing processes. Examples include complex application forms, multi-step verification, and deliberately confusing cancellation processes.
details.whyItMatters: While nudges make good behavior easier, sludge makes beneficial actions harder. Government sludge prevents eligible citizens from receiving benefits, and corporate sludge traps customers in unwanted services.
takeaways: Sludge is excessive friction that prevents people from achieving their goals
Government sludge reduces program uptake among eligible beneficiaries
Corporate sludge deliberately makes cancellation and refunds difficult

faq.question: How does sludge differ from a legitimate process requirement?
faq.answer: Legitimate friction serves a valid purpose like identity verification or informed consent. Sludge is friction that serves no purpose except to discourage action. The test is whether the friction benefits the person going through it or the institution imposing it.

faq.question: What are common examples of government sludge?
faq.answer: Multi-page benefit applications requiring documentation the government already has, in-person appointments for tasks that could be done online, annual re-enrollment in ongoing programs, and deadline-based forfeiture of earned benefits.
